paper_title: EmbodiedSWE: Coding Agents for Long Horizon Dexterous Robotics

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We study coding agents for long-horizon, dexterous robotics and ask whether their solutions can provide scalable supervision for learning general robot policies. To test this, we develop EMBODIEDSWE-BENCH, a simulation benchmark for coding agents spanning contact-rich manipulation, deformable objects, and long-horizon tasks requiring up to half an hour of continuous interaction. We find that frontier coding agents can solve complex long-horizon tasks and transfer prior solutions across both tasks and embodiments. We also design supporting tools that help agents more effectively solve these tasks. However, the resulting solutions require substantial iterative interaction and are typically specialized to individual task instances. We therefore introduce EMBODIEDSWE-GEN, which expands a single solution from coding agent into large diverse trajectories for training a VLA. VLA performance improves with more generated demonstrations, and agent-aided diversification improves generalization to held-out task variations. We also show that a VLA finetuned solely on coding-agent-generated simulation demonstrations completes a long-horizon task on real robot. Together, our framework uses coding agents to solve complex robotics tasks and turn verified solutions into scalable supervision for robot policies.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: A longstanding goal in robotics is generalist robot that can act autonomously in daily life, solving wide range of dexterous and long-horizon tasks. Imagine robot that can construct house completely autonomously; this requires months of coordinated work from fine-grained woodworking, to furniture assembly, to electrical wiring. true generalist robot could do all of these components continuously for days or weeks. Yet current approaches remain far from achieving this goal. Vision-language-action (VLA) models, for example, learn from demonstrations (Intelligence et al., 2025; NVIDIA et al., 2025; Team et al., 2025), but collecting such data at scale remains expensive (Tian et al., 2025). Teleoperation requires many human operators and can be difficult to scale. And learning directly from human video demonstrations can result in mismatches with real robot embodiments. For precise interactions such as screw threading, tight insertion, or grasping in deeply cluttered environments, collecting demonstrations can be prohibitively difficult. Recently, coding agents have offered new paradigm: they write, execute, inspect, and revise robot control programs much like human engineers, turning robot programming into an iterative process of action and reflection. Existing work remains largely constrained to navigation and pick-and-place tasks (Fu et al., 2026; Mu et al., 2024; Singh et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2023), often relying on human-designed interfaces such as object-pose queries or macro primitives that constrain the task *Project leads with equal contribution. Figure 1: Overview of our framework: Top: EMBODIEDSWE-BENCH contains diverse longhorizon robotics tasks. Bottom: coding agents solve these tasks and turn verified solutions into scalable supervision for general policies. space. Progress is also difficult to measure. Real-hardware iteration is expensive (Xiao et al., 2026; Fu et al., 2026), while simulation benchmarks rarely combine long horizon tasks with challenging physical interactions (like dextrous manipulation). This raises question: can coding agents solve long-horizon dexterous tasks in way that creates scalable and transferable demonstration data for bootstrapping generalist policies? We examine this question in three parts. First, we build benchmark of daily-life tasks, EMBODIEDSWE-BENCH, including problems that take tens of minutes to solve and involve contact-intensive manipulation, deformable objects, liquids, and cutting. For example, the benchmark tests whether coding agent can create solution program for cutting food, assembling an Ikea table, and packing away tools into drawer. Second, we test whether coding agents can create full solutions to the problems in EMBODIEDSWEBENCH when given access to the full simulator state. And we find that frontier agents can find solutions to many of these problemsfrom 11% success rate on GPT-5.6 Terra to 82% on GPT6 Astra. We also show that giving access to additional tools as part of the harness can improve performance further in some cases. This shows that coding agents could potentially be used to create precomputed solutions to complex long-horizon problems, with little intervention. Third, we test whether these coding agent solutions can help bootstrap generalist policies, like VLAs. We create hierarchical pipeline, EMBODIEDSWE-GEN, with data augmentation and other improvements, that creates teacher demonstrations from the coding agent solutions. We find that VLA success rates improve with the amount of demonstrations from the coding agent pipeline, and even improve out-of-distribution success rates more than baseline domain randomization approaches. We further demonstrate sim-to-real transfer: policy finetuned solely on 500 codingagent-generated simulation demonstrations completes four-stage lamp-disassembly task. Together our work shows potential path forward for scaling demonstrations and leveraging coding agents to create optimal solutions to long-horizon, complex problems. To summarize our work has three contributions: (1) EMBODIEDSWE-BENCH, benchmark for evaluating coding agents on long-horizon, dexterous daily-life robotics tasks with realistic dynamics; (2) coding agents as solvers, with systematic evaluation of frontier agents on robotics tasks; (3) coding agents as teachers, with hierarchical data engine EMBODIEDSWE-GEN that transforms verified solutions into large, diverse datasets for VLA finetuning.

sections.title: 1.1 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Recent work studies coding agents as robot programmers, including benchmarking across different levels of perception and control abstraction (Fu et al., 2026), discovering reusable skills for robotics 2 Preprint. Figure 2: Representative successful trajectories from coding-agent solutions on EMBODIEDSWEBENCH, spanning long-horizon manipulation across tasks and embodiments. tasks (Lu et al., 2026), and improving policies through real-robot interaction (Xiao et al., 2026). Separately, simulation data pipelines generate demonstrations by adapting human trajectories (Mandlekar et al., 2023), using language models to assist task and policy generation (Hua et al., 2024), or composing scripted skills (Tian et al., 2025). We connect these directions by studying coding agents as both task solvers and demonstration generators. EMBODIEDSWE-BENCH emphasizes longhorizon tasks with demanding physical interactions. Starting from verified agent-written solutions in code, EMBODIEDSWE-GEN uses an agent-aided pipeline to scalably generate diverse trajectories as demonstrations for robot learning. Thus, agents contribute both the solution and diversified trajectories, which we evaluate as supervision for VLA training. We present detailed discussions of related works in Appendix A.

sections.title: 2 EMBODIEDSWE-BENCH
sections.content: EMBODIEDSWE-BENCH is simulation benchmark designed to test diverse range of dexterous and long-horizon tasks. We describe the environment design and evaluation protocol below; the full task catalog and additional details are provided in Appendix B.

sections.title: 2.1 ENVIRONMENT DESIGN
sections.content: We construct 28 long-horizon and dexterous tasks spanning assembly (9), packing (4), puzzle (6), deformable object or liquid manipulation (4), cutting (2), and locomotion with manipulation (3). Examples include assembling an Ikea table with four legs, securing motherboard with seven bolts, and tying shoelace half knot. Tasks demand precise physical interactions and execution horizons of up to half an hour. The benchmark supports five embodiments: Franka, UFACTORY xArm7, Kinova Gen3, bimanual Franka, and Unitree G1. Some examples can be found in Figure 2. Task design and reference-solution development are primarily human driven, with coding-agent assistance. Scenes use Isaac Lab, Isaac Sim robot assets, and downloaded, scanned, CAD-derived, or custom-modeled objects. Agents have access to full simulator states, generic rendering and inspection tools, and configurable controllers, including operational-space and inverse-kinematics control. Humanoid locomotion uses pretrained policy. Appendix provides implementation details.

sections.title: 2.2 EVALUATION PROTOCOL
sections.content: Each evaluation run is executed in an isolated Docker container with preinstalled Python environment and simulator. The agent receives only minimal task-specific copy of the benchmark, the task instruction, and fresh workspace; all other resources are inaccessible, with network access restricted to the model API and Python package index. The required deliverable is Python program exposing solve(env) as its entry point. The agent may submit intermediate solutions, and submissions are also triggered automatically at fixed intervals. 3 Preprint. Figure 3: Base results on EMBODIEDSWE-BENCH. Left, middle: mean best-so-far score over 28 tasks against wall-clock and tokens; markers with vertical bars at hourly intervals / fixed token counts show mean SEM across tasks (one run per task). Right: mean final score with SEM across tasks; percentages give the fraction of tasks solved. Grading is performed entirely offline to prevent agents from modifying scene code or exploiting the reward mechanism. Each submission is evaluated in separate grading environment with identical scene dynamics, while state-writing interfaces such as set states() are disabled to preserve physical consistency. task-specific grader is used. In some tasks, simulator information is used for gradingfor example if an object is in the right place. In others, human-written rubric is used, combined with VLM, to grade the trajectory or subcomponents of the trajectory.

sections.title: 3 EVALUATING CODING AGENTS AS SOLVERS
sections.content: Having established the benchmark and evaluation protocol, we study coding agents as robotic task solvers. Each agent iteratively inspects the environment, executes candidate solutions, diagnoses failures, and revises its code, optimizing program rather than the parameters of learned policy. We first evaluate frontier coding agents using their standard coding harnesses (Section 3.1), then examine transfer learning capability across tasks and robot embodiments (Section 3.2), and finally describe additional tools for long-horizon solving (Section 3.3). We also explore training coding agents on synthetic robotics tasks. We present the automatic task construction pipeline and preliminary agentic RL results in Appendix G.

sections.title: 3.1 FRONTIER AGENT CAPABILITIES
sections.content: Standard-harness performance. We evaluate six frontier models on EMBODIEDSWE-BENCH: Fable 5.1, Opus 5, Opus 4.8, GPT-6 Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol, and GPT-5.6 Terra. Each model uses its native coding harness: the first three use Claude Code, while the latter three use Codex. The additional long-horizon mechanisms introduced later in Section 3.3 are disabled. Unless otherwise stated, all experiments follow the protocol in Section 2.2. Each run uses one NVIDIA RTX 4090 for simulation and 4-hour wall-clock budget. At each wall-clock budget, we report the highest graded score achieved by the run up to that point and average across runs (mean standard error). Wall-clock time includes simulation. Despite this difficulty, frontier coding agents make substantial progress within the 4-hour budget, with the strongest model solving roughly 80% of the benchmark. The remaining failures are concentrated among some of the most challenging tasks. These tasks are not inherently infeasible: every evaluated task has been successfully completed at least once by domain expert working with coding model. The gap therefore highlights the difficulty of autonomously discovering successful programs for the hardest tasks under fixed interaction budget. Failure modes. We also identify several recurring failure modes when coding agents solve robotics tasks. Poor visual grounding. Agents sometimes rely primarily on printed simulator states rather than inspecting rendered observations, leading them to misjudge task progress or leave the robot in physically pathological configurations. Over-commitment to failing plan. Agents may lock into an incorrect task decomposition early and interpret subsequent failures only as parametertuning problems, rather than reconsidering the underlying strategy. Scorer hacking. Some agents attempt to improve the score without solving the task through the robot, for example by directly modifying object poses through set states() or write root pose to sim), applying external forces or torques to manipulated objects, or exploiting scene-side actuation channels. We present detailed evaluation and aggregation results in Appendix C.1, including per-task and permodel summaries, breakdowns by difficulty, suite, and embodiment, score curves against time and tokens, resource use, and reward-hack statistics. We provide concrete agent trajectory as example for each of the failure modes described above in Appendix H. Coding Agent Policies vs Learned Control Policies. One could imagine learning demonstration solutions to these simulations via tabula rasa reinforcement learning, rather than coding agents. As such, we further compare the programmatic policies produced by coding agents with policies trained, through Proximal Policy Optimization (Schulman et al., 2017) on subset of EMBODIEDSWE-BENCH with similar wall-clock times as the coding agents. This uses small MLP-based policy with access to the simulator state (in the style of prior control benchmarks like (Tassa et al., 2018)). We consider three reward design mechanisms of increasing supervision: (1) sparse, using only the progress signals defined by the evaluation rubric; (2) agent-designed dense, where frontier coding agent constructs task-specific dense rewards; and (3) expert-tuned, where domain expert1 works together with frontier model to refine the rewards, hyperparameters, and relevant environment settings. Because PPO training is substantially more expensive than executing programmatic policy, reward and training design are performed offline rather than counted against the agents solving budget. For the latter two settings, we allow repeated development and tuning over approximately one week and report the best resulting training configuration. Since expert-inthe-loop tuning is costly, we restrict this comparison to five tasks spanning the assembly and packing suites. Full task selections, reward definitions, hyperparameters, and tuning procedures are provided in Appendix C.2. Figure 5 summarizes the results. Despite stronger supervision and extensive offline tuning, learning tabula rasa with PPO still substantially underperforms the programmatic policies discovered by coding agents within the same wall-clock time. sections.title: 3.2 TRANSFER ACROSS TASKS AND EMBODIMENTS
sections.content: Verified solutions often provide useful experience for subsequent problems, even when the tasks are only loosely related: prior solution can encode reusable task structure as well as embodimentspecific knowledge, such as reliable grasp configurations, approach poses, or controller settings. We study this transfer systematically across both tasks and robot embodiments. We evaluate Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol, with three seeds per configuration. In each transfer run, the agent receives, in addition to the standard task materials, one read-only file containing either verified solution to another task or verified solution to the same task on different embodiment. We compare against otherwise identical runs without this reference. Full task pairings, run counts, per-task curves, and token-based analyses are provided in Appendix C. Transfer across tasks. For transfer across tasks, we select 6 target tasks and pair each with 2 source tasks: similar source that shares the targets dominant underlying skill (e.g., threading, card seating), and dissimilar source that does not; the exact pairs are listed in Appendix C. Figure 6 shows the results. Hints from similar tasks help the agent solve the target both better and faster; hints from dissimilar tasks speed up early progress but end at the same final score as the no-hint runs. Transfer across embodiments. For transfer across embodiments, we use the same 6 tasks. For each task, we provide the verified Franka-arm solution as the hint and instruct the agent to solve the task on two other embodiments: Kinova Gen3 and UFACTORY xArm7, each carrying the Franka Panda hand so that grasping is comparable while the arm kinematics, joint layout, reach, and control gains all change. As the no-hint reference, we reuse the Franka runs on these six tasks from the cross-task experiments. Figure 6 shows that solution transfer is efficient and achieves higher scores than this reference, suggesting that agents reuse task decomposition and scene reasoning while adapting motion and control to the new embodiment.

sections.title: 3.3 ABLATING ADDITIONAL TOOLS FOR SOLVING LONG-HORIZON ROBOTICS TASKS
sections.content: Beyond the standard coding harnesses evaluated in Section 3.1, we provide additional tools designed to support long-horizon, physically complex task solving. Full descriptions of these tools are provided in Appendix C.4. This includes: Checkpoint tree. The agent saves reached simulator states together with the programs, logs, snapshots, and transition annotations that document its progress as tree of checkpoints. The agent can go to any previous checkpoints, allowing the agent to revisit earlier decisions without replaying long prefixes or losing the record of failed attempts. Evolutionary search on parameters. For fixed program structure, the agent specifies tunable parameters, search ranges, and an objective. The tool runs CMA-ES (Hansen, 2023) over par6 Preprint. Starting from one verified coding-agent solution, we diversify the scene, strategy, phase, dynamics, and visual to expand it into broad set of training trajectories. Higher-level variations modify task structure, solution behavior, and intermediate-state coverage, while lower-level variations introduce physical, action, and visual perturbations to improve robustness and diversify execution. allel simulations initialized from common starting state, optionally with initial-state jitter to reduce overfitting, and returns the best parameters found. Other supporting tools. We also provide several other supporting tools that we find useful to the agents: scene viewer provides snapshots and videos for visual inspection; sweep tool compares alternative programs or strategies in parallel; and an assessment log records structured descriptions of the scene, failures, and suspicious outcomes after each execution. We evaluate Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol on our full benchmark using the same set up as in Section 3.1 with tools, and compare with the performance without tools. Each tool run uses two RTX 4090s rather than one; the second hosts the parallel simulations of the parameter search and the sweep tool. The results are presented in Figure 6. We can see that both models are able to achieve better score with the tools, though effect sizes are relatively small. We present detailed results in Appendix and some qualitative analysis in Appendix H.

sections.title: 4 CODING AGENTS AS TEACHERS
sections.content: Section 3 demonstrated that coding agents are capable of solving complex, long-horizon robotic tasks through iterative reasoning, execution, and debugging. These successful solutions provide more than task completion alone: they also contain structured action sequences and reusable interaction strategies. We next ask whether such agent-generated solutions can be used as supervision to train general robot policy.

sections.title: 4.1 SCALABLE DATA ENGINE
sections.content: Generating diverse robot trajectories at scale is challenging because single coding-agent solution can require hours of wall-clock time and substantial token cost. Purely rule or script based generation 7 Preprint. is cheaper, but its diversity can quickly saturate around narrow regime. We therefore propose an agent-powered data engine, EMBODIEDSWE-GEN, that expands each verified solution with both agent-based diversification and standard domain randomization. We show representative examples of this diversification in Figure 7 and describe the details of our pipeline in Appendix D. (3) Phase: (2) Strategy: Agent-based diversification. The agent edits the task and solution code in four ways. (1) Scene: it varies objects, tools, distractors, and workspace layouts, updating the success condition and solution as needed. it changes the order of interchangeable steps, grasp choices, or the overall task plan, and adds recovery branches such as regrasping dropped to cover intermediate states object. that are rarely visited by end-to-end rollouts, the agent generates demonstrations that begin partway through task. It identifies phase boundaries, constructs diverse valid simulator states for those intermediate stages, and adapts the solution to complete the remaining steps from each state. (4) Noise: single noise scale can be too weak during transport yet too disruptive during precise manipulation. The agent adapts DART-style noise injection (Laskey et al., 2017) to the task by inspecting rendered rollout and writing phase-specific perturbations into the solution code, for example using stronger disturbances during transport and weaker ones during insertion. These disturbances can trigger the solutions recovery branches. Figure 8: One verified solution can be expanded into many diverse trajectories through hierarchical diversification, with only modest additional agent cost per variation and rapidly decreasing amortized cost at scale. Domain randomization. We use scripts to sample two further types of variation from ranges specified by the agent. (1) Physical parameters: mass, friction, and contact properties. (2) Visual: lighting, texture, background and camera poses are varied offline by re-rendering recorded states, producing additional visual observations of the same physical trajectories. Generated trajectories are retained only if they pass the task grader and an open-loop replay check.

sections.title: 4.2 VLA FINETUNING WITH GENERATED DEMONSTRATIONS
sections.content: We next test whether trajectories produced by EMBODIEDSWE-GEN provide effective supervision for VLA finetuning. Since several benchmark tasks remain beyond current VLAs, we evaluate SmolVLA (Shukor et al., 2025) on subset of six tasks: clear organic objects, pen holder, tool packing, bulb, nut thread, and slice. We study two questions: how performance scales with the number of generated demonstrations, and whether trajectory diversification improves generalization. Training details and task-specific evaluation criteria are provided in Appendix E. Scaling with generated demonstrations. We subsample the generated trajectories at 10, 50, 100, 200, and 400 demonstrations per task to finetune VLA and evaluate in distribution, using the same scene and initial-state distribution as the generated data. Figure 9 shows that task scores and success rates improve overall with more demonstrations: the mean success rate over the six tasks rises from 18% with 10 demonstrations to 69% with 400, and the mean rubric score from 0.32 to 0.76. Generalization across diversification pipelines. We evaluate whether agent-aided diversification improves generalization. We compare policies trained on equal numbers of demonstrations generated by our pipeline or script-only baseline using standard domain randomization, noise, and small initial-state perturbations. The script-only baseline remains concentrated around the original task distribution, whereas agent-aided diversification introduces broader variation in scenes, solution strategies, and initial configurations. Both policies are evaluated on the same held-out test set, which contains semantically novel task instances and geometric configurations unseen during training. For example, in food-slicing task, agent-aided training data may include bananas, carrots, and cucumbers in varied placements, while the test set contains unseen object categories, such as bread, chilli, and zucchini, in previously unseen initial configurations. sections.title: 5 DISCUSSIONS AND CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduced EMBODIEDSWE-BENCH, benchmark of long-horizon, dexterous daily-life tasks in which the agent writes code directly against the simulator. We find that frontier coding agents can already solve wide range of complex tasks from scratch and transfer verified solutions across tasks and embodiments, though the hardest tasks remain unsolved. Verified solutions then serve as supervision for robot learning: with EMBODIEDSWE-GEN, we turn each solution into large, diverse dataset for fine-tuning general robot policy. Together, these results show how coding agents can solve complex robotics tasks and provide scalable supervision for robot policies, with demonstrated sim-to-real transfer.

sections.title: A RELATED WORK
sections.content: Coding agents as robot programmers. recent line of work has coding agents solve manipulation tasks by operating human-built interface, which primarily measures how well the agent can understand the physical world through that interface. CaP-X (Fu et al., 2026) is the reference benchmark, with different tiers of API access. In the most assisted tier, the agent has access to groundtruth simulation states with human-written macros. Other tiers include curated wrappers over vision models and planners. Some follow-up works keep the interface and vary the loop around it, e.g., skill libraries with evolutionary program search (Lu et al., 2026), training-time evolution of policy repositories (Elmaaroufi et al., 2026), real-robot self-improvement inside human-built reset and verification modules (Xiao et al., 2026), and tool-calling over frozen planners and VLAs (Galanti et al., 2026). Results are polarized, with some easy cube tasks almost saturated while several LIBERO-Pro long-horizon tasks having zero success (Lu et al., 2026). These interfaces bring problems of their own: each is task-specific, e.g., CaP-X reimplements get object pose per task family, down to hardcoded object names. The vision-backed tiers inject perception noise that can compound and make otherwise correct programs fail. These works also treat the agents code as the endpoint, i.e., the deployed policy itself, as opposed to teacher. We remove human-designed interfaces on long-horizon tasks and find that frontier coding agents (e.g., Claude Fable 5) already write working solutions from scratch against Isaac Sim. We harvest these solutions as training data for policies that fail there. Long-horizon manipulation. Long-horizon tasks are consistent failure mode for robot policies: VLA policies degrade most on the long-horizon suites of standard benchmarks (Liu et al., 2023; Tsui et al., 2026), the strongest agentic systems have zero success on several LIBERO-Pro long-horizon tasks (Lu et al., 2026), and the 2025 BEHAVIOR Challenge was won at 12.4% success rate despite 1,200 hours of teleoperated demonstrations (Larchenko et al., 2025; Bai et al., 2025). Previous works improve performance of robot policies on long-horizon tasks with both inference-time and training-time approaches. Inference-time approaches often decompose the task: Gemini Robotics 1.5 interleaves natural-language reasoning with acting to break down multi-step tasks (Team et al., 2025), (Zhang & Shah, 2026; Kwok et al., 2025) use verifier to select optimal actions through best-of-N to steering the inference-time performance. Hi Robot puts VLM planner over lowlevel policy (Shi et al., 2025), and Pigey runs an orchestration loop with explicit memory over frozen skills (Galanti et al., 2026). Training-time approaches instead supply long-horizon data: π0.5 reaches multi-minute behaviors through heterogeneous co-training (Intelligence et al., 2025), and InternData-A1s ablation shows that removing its long-horizon slice hurts pre-training more than removing pick-and-place entirely (Tian et al., 2025). Automatic data generation in simulation. large body of work automates parts of the simulation data pipeline, but every method multiplies or perturbs something human first supplied, and that input caps the horizon of what it can generate. Task and scene generators need human to write the task schema, label per-asset keypoints for hand-built motion planner, define reward templates for per-subtask RL, or teleoperate seed demonstrations (Wang et al., 2024a; Hua et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024b; Nasiriany et al., 2024). InternData-A1 provides evidence that simulation alone suffices for VLA pre-training and identifies trajectory diversity as possibly crucial to pre-training quality; yet it produces data by chaining hand-engineered scripted skills under human-authored per-task configuration (Tian et al., 2025). Related works extend the recipe in different directions, including synthesizing tasks together with executable success checks (Wang et al., 2026a), co-training on neurally generated trajectories (NVIDIA et al., 2025), or rolling trajectories out inside learned world models (Guo et al., 2026). Prior demonstration synthesis pipelines have similar dependence on human demonstrations: the MimicGen family turns 10 teleoperated demonstrations per task into thousands by SE(3) transform-and-replay of recorded segments with success filtering (Mandlekar et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2025; Garrett et al., 2024); broad family of methods synthesizes new demonstrations by varying human-provided seeds (Xue et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025; Ravan et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026); QDTraj applies quality-diversity to trajectories over low-dimensional, human-parameterized pose genotype (Kappel et al., 2026). Some recent works begin to hand scene and environment generation itself to agents (Ranawaka et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b; Kang et al., 2026). 16 Preprint. Physics are simulated with PhysX through Isaac Lab, using 10ms time the four deformable-object tasks (tshirt, dumpling, step and the TGS solver by default; shoe knot, latte) run on Isaac Labs Newton backend instead. Scenes may override these defaults to accommodate their contact geometry. In particular, the threaded-assembly scenes (nut thread, allen bolt, pc motherboard, and ikea table) model explicit thread engagement using signed-distance-field collision meshes and therefore use higher solver iteration counts and larger GPU contact buffers. Embodiment-specific presets may further adjust these settings. Each control step advances the simulation by several physics substeps, as determined by the controllers decimation. Scene-specific mechanics, such as the syringes plunger-liquid coupling, are updated at every substep. Randomization. Each scene defines distribution over reset conditions, and each graded episode is sampled from that distribution. For example, in coffee, the capsule and mug are initialized at their tray slots with 2cm of horizontal jitter and random yaw; the brew duration is also sampled. In pen holder, the number of pens present is sampled per episode, and the holder and all present pens are placed with 4cm of horizontal jitter and random yaw. Each scene records its randomization ranges in its configuration. Agents develop against fixed seed but are explicitly informed that grading uses different initial conditions. Assets. Robot models are vendored from the Isaac Sim asset library and patched locally as needed. For example, the stock xArm7 gripper attachment declares second articulation root, which we remove in our copy. Task objects are downloaded, scanned, or hand-modeled assets included with the benchmark. Offline vendoring scripts derive asset-specific constants, including grasp bands, rest heights, and mouth frames. The resulting values are recorded in the corresponding scene source. 18 Preprint. The baselines share one training and grading stack; the three conditions differ only in who writes the reward and whether the environment is adapted to it. Tasks. We train on five single-arm Franka tasks: bulb, nut thread, slice, pen holder, and tool packing. These span the assembly, cutting, and packing suites and use the same regis28 Preprint. tered presets as the agent runs. The tasks are drawn from the easier tiers of EMBODIEDSWE-BENCH  (Table 3)  and have relatively few rubric stages, so they favor RL: each rubric has two or three stages, and the first stage is pick in every case. Performance is graded with the same rubric score as the agent runs. In addition, we manually inspect every graded trajectory for reward hacking and deduct the score of any stage that was reached without genuinely performing it. Observation and action. The observation is the concatenation of the flattened full simulator state returned by the environments get states() (in environment-local coordinates, with actuator setpoints and controller state dropped), the end-effector pose and velocity, and the previous action. We additionally apply PPOs running observation normalization. Actions are normalized to [1, 1] and mapped affinely onto the preset controllers command range; finger dimensions map to perfinger position targets in metres. Reward construction. Across all RL conditions, the per-step reward combines task-specific potential ϕ(st) [0, 1] with binary success bonus: rt = (ϕ(st) + 1[successt]) t, where denotes the control period. Success and the stage-progress curves reported in our analysis are determined by the task grader. Episodes use fixed horizon and do not terminate upon success. The three RL conditions differ only in how the potential ϕ is constructed. Sparse. ϕ is given by the graders weighted rubric progress. This provides RL with privileged signal that is never exposed to the coding agent. Because the policy can occasionally increase rubric progress without actually completing the intended stagefor example, by knocking the bulb upward and transiently satisfying the lifted height thresholdwe manually inspect RL rollouts for reward hacking. Any spuriously triggered stage is removed from the reported score. We apply this correction consistently across all evaluation within this test. Agent-designed dense. frontier coding agent proposes task-specific dense potential itself, written as weighted sum of stage terms over the scenes public accessors (part poses, tolerances, and the hand pose), and iterates on it offline for about one week against training runs. Table 15 lists the final reward proposed by the agent after these offline iterations. Expert-tuned. domain expert working with frontier model iterates on the reward, the environment, and the training hyperparameters for about one week, with the goal of reaching as high rubric score as possible. Table 16 summarizes the reward terms and the weights used in training, Table 17 summarizes the environment changes for each task, and Table 18 summarizes the fine-tuned training hyperparameters. Algorithm and hyperparameters. We use PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) as implemented in rsl rl (Rudin et al., 2022) with the Isaac Lab manipulation defaults, uniform across tasks: 1,024 parallel environments, actor and critic MLPs with hidden sizes (256, 128, 64) and ELU activations, running observation normalization, initial action noise standard deviation 1.0, 64 steps per environment per iteration, 4 passes over each collected rollout batch with 4 mini-batches per pass, clipping parameter 0.2, GAE with γ = 0.99 and λ = 0.95, value-loss coefficient 1.0, adaptive learning rate starting at 104 with KL target of 0.016, gradient-norm clipping at 1.0, and no entropy bonus. The sparse and dense conditions use these values unchanged; the expert-tuned condition overrides them per task  (Table 18)  . Evaluation protocol. Each run trains on single RTX 4090, and every condition is trained with three seeds per task. Checkpoints are saved at every whole hour of training; each is exported as TorchScript policy and graded via the standard evaluation protocol described in Section 2.2. Each grade takes 32 trials with fixed evaluation seed, and the average is reported. We additionally manually check each recorded grading trajectory and correct the score for reward hacking. C.4 HARNESS DETAILS We describe the tools summarized in Section 3.3. These tools complement the agents native coding and debugging capabilities. Checkpoint tree. Long-horizon task solving benefits from preserving intermediate progress and revisiting earlier decisions. We organize exploration as tree: each node represents simulator state reached by the agent and maintains record of the branches attempted from that state. Whenever the agent judges that its current progress is worth preserving, it can checkpoint the complete simulator state to disk as child of its current node. The checkpoint also stores the exact program that produced the state, the programs full printed logs, and camera snapshot. Each node carries three transition annotations. First, the agent provides natural-language description of the action that led from the parent node to the current node. Second, the tool automatically compares the two saved states, recording object displacements, rotations, and joint changes beyond 32 Preprint. Figure 18: Cross-embodiment generalization by task. Rubric score versus agent wall-clock time (mean SEM over 2 models 3 seeds) for the two target embodiments given the Franka reference solution as hint. From-scratch Franka runs are shown as reference for task difficulty. tolerance, as well as quantities that did not change. Third, the agent describes the visual scene difference after inspecting the parent and current snapshots. The agent can backtrack to any saved node. The tool restores the simulator state and returns the record of every branch already attempted from that node, including the code, action descriptions, and induced state and scene differences. This preserves the context needed to reconsider earlier decisions and avoid repeating attempts that have already failed. Evolutionary search on parameters. Solution programs often contain constants such as rotation angles, torque limits, and per-step insertion increments. An agent may discover suitable program structure but spend substantial time tuning these constants through sequential reruns. We therefore provide an evolutionary search tool that optimizes parameters while keeping the program structure fixed. The agent specifies the parameters to search, range for each, and an objective to minimize. For example, when seating leg, the objective can be the remaining insertion depth plus the lateral offset from the slot. The tool constructs batched instance of the task with 512 parallel environments by default, initializes every environment at the state from which the search begins, and runs CMAES (Hansen, 2023) over the declared ranges. Parameter specifications support floating-point and integer ranges, logarithmic scaling, and categorical choices. The agents current parameter values are included as candidate in the first generation, so the best evaluated candidate is no worse than this baseline on the search objective. To reduce overfitting to single starting configuration, the tool can jitter the starting states of named objects independently across environments and average each candidates objective over several jittered repeats. By default, the search runs for eight generations. It returns the best parameters found, per-parameter sensitivity estimate, and warning whenever best value lies at the boundary of its declared range. Scene viewer. The scene viewer captures snapshots and videos of program execution, allowing the agent to inspect outcomes visually rather than relying solely on numerical simulator states. 33 Preprint. Sweep tool. The sweep tool executes several candidate programs simultaneously using Isaacs simulation parallelism. Unlike parameter search, it supports comparisons between different program structures or task-solving strategies. Assessment log. After each program execution, the assessment log persists short structured verdict describing the scene, what failed, and what appears suspicious. This encourages closer examination of both simulator states and rendered observations during subsequent diagnosis and revision. 34 Preprint. EMBODIEDSWE-GEN DETAILS In this section, we describe the details of our data engine EMBODIEDSWE-GEN. The engine has three stages: diversification, batched generation, and automatic verification and augmentation. Its core is offline diversification: coding agent expands each verified solution along five levels, proposing semantic variations together with the corresponding code or state perturbations. These variants are then composed and rolled out in massively parallel simulation to generate trajectories at scale. Finally, failed or low-quality trajectories are filtered out, while retained trajectories are augmented with additional supervision, such as task progress and natural-language descriptions of the current situation and intended goal. Much of this annotation can be derived directly from the solution program and simulator state through scripted processing, making it substantially cheaper than labeling each generated trajectory post hoc with humans (Lynch et al., 2023; Sermanet et al., 2023) or foundation models (Xiao et al., 2023; Zawalski et al., 2024). Section D.1 describes the five levels of hierarchical diversification; Section D.2 describes how generation run is orchestrated and verified; Section D.3 describes what run delivers. D.1 DIVERSIFICATION LEVELS Scene. The agent edits the scene code and task configuration by varying objects, tools, or workspace conditions. Examples include replacing the knife used for cutting, swapping the food item to be diced, adding more objects to tabletop-cleaning task, introducing distractors or obstacles, or rearranging the workspace. When necessary, the agent also updates the corresponding success condition and solution strategy. Edits that would change the tasks contact-critical mechanics (thread geometry, insertion channels, fastening) are not permitted, and the delivered solve must still succeed in the new scene. Strategy. The agent directly modifies the solution code to produce alternative strategies at three levels of granularity: solver parameters, such as applied force or clearance; local decisions, such as grasp locations or the ordering of interchangeable steps; and qualitatively different plans that change the overall task strategy. The agent may also introduce recovery branches to recover from off-nominal states created by noise perturbations, such as returning to grasping phase after an object is dropped. Only the latter two count as new strategies for the purpose of the strategy gate (Section D.2); parameter changes on the same motion are kept as arguments of an existing solution. Phase. As tasks become longer, agent-generated solutions naturally decompose into multiple phases. However, successful rollouts from the default initial state typically cover only narrow subset of the intermediate state space. We therefore ask the agent to identify phase boundaries, propose diverse valid initial conditions for each intermediate phase, and solve directly from those states, substantially expanding coverage of states that are rarely encountered in end-to-end rollouts. Concretely, the agent writes one initial-state builder per phase and version of the solution that can be entered at any phase; at generation time the builder constructs the initial state and the solution runs from there to completion under the tasks grader. Dynamics. We diversify dynamics in two ways. First, we randomize physical parameters such as mass, friction, and contact properties. The agent declares, once per scene, the ranges over which these parameters may vary (with the nominal values reproducing the original scene); at generation time each parallel environment draws its own values. Second, we perturb the executed actions to induce local trajectory variation, using either small DART-style noise (Laskey et al., 2017) at each step or larger disturbances applied over short intervals. Which perturbation to apply where is decided by the agent: it is shown rendered episode of the task, identifies the phases in which the motion is free (transport, approach) and those in which it is tolerance-critical (grasping, mating, insertion), and writes per-phase disturbance into the solution through dedicated argument, env.step(action, noise=). The recorder logs the clean command and executes the perturbed one. For position-mode controllers the clean command is the training label, so labels remain unperturbed while the recorded trajectory shows the recovery; for torque-mode controllers the label is the achieved next-step joint position, which does reflect the perturbation (Appendix D.3). The perturbation is scaled by pipeline-controlled factor that is zero during authoring and verification 35 Preprint. and non-zero only during the dynamics harvest. These perturbations can produce off-nominal states and invoke the recovery behaviors introduced at the strategy level. Visual. We diversify visual appearance by varying camera parameters, lighting, textures, and backgrounds. Because these changes do not affect the underlying dynamics, they can be applied offline to recorded trajectories at rendering cost only. The agent declares, once per scene, the cameras and the ranges of the render-only parameters (lighting intensity and color temperature, table and background materials, object albedo where it does not carry task-relevant identity); appearance that the grader or the task depends on is not randomized. Rendering is then fully script-driven: each verified trajectory is re-rendered under several draws from these ranges through the scenes cameras. D.2 GENERATION AND VERIFICATION Input and trajectory targets. run starts from the tasks environment preset and verified solution folder containing solve.py and its supporting modules. It first obtains one successful nominal trajectory, then expands the accepted set through scene, strategy, phase, and dynamics diversification. Collection targets vary across tasks; they do not specify the number of distinct scenes, strategies, or phases. Each set contains the preceding set in full. The visual stage renders the accepted trajectories under multiple appearance settings, producing additional dataset episodes. Variant organization. The run maintains its own copies of the scene, grader, and solution code. Variants are organized by scene, strategy, and, when applicable, starting phase. scene variant contains its scene and grader; strategy variant supplies solution for scene; and phase variant supplies initial-state builders and solution that can start at an intermediate phase. We call runnable combination of scene, strategy, and optional starting phase cell. Recorded trajectories identify their source cell and the fingerprint of its code at recording time. Initial checks. Before diversification, the input solution must succeed in single environment and pass the replay check described below. It must also complete batch of 512 parallel environments with at least one success that passes replay at the same batch size. Failure of the single-environment check starts an agent session to repair the solution; failure of the batched check starts session to adapt it for parallel execution. These checks and any required sessions share 12-hour time budget. Acceptance and selection. At each of the scene, strategy, and phase stages, the agent creates and tests variants until the trajectory target is met. stage must introduce at least one new cell, and every new cell it retains must produce at least one successful trajectory that passes replay. Newly recorded trajectories count only if their source code is unchanged since recording; an edited cell therefore needs new successful recordings. Previously accepted sets are retained unchanged when later stages edit the source code. Once the acceptance conditions are met, the orchestrator retains the preceding set and fills the remaining places by taking trajectories in turn from the available cells, giving priority to cells introduced at the current stage. Byte-identical trajectory files count only once, and newly created cells with code identical to an existing cell are removed. These checks reject exact duplicates; the authoring instructions specify the intended differences between strategies. This selection procedure distributes the available places across working variants instead of filling them from single prolific solution. Replay verification. recorded success is accepted only if it passes an open-loop action replay check. The checker rebuilds the recording batch with the same scene, number of parallel environments, seed, and per-environment physical parameters. It restores the recorded initial states and controller settings, including gains, control period, nullspace posture, gripper stiffness, and any changes to these settings made during execution. Changes are reapplied at their recorded steps. The checker then replays the recorded action sequence without running the solution program and requires the tasks grader to report success again. Replay processes the whole recording batch together, keeping each trajectory in its original environment slot to preserve the batch configuration. failed replay excludes the trajectory. During recorded execution, solutions are required to affect the world through env.step; direct state 36 Preprint. changes, external forces, and separate drive commands would introduce effects outside the recorded actions. Initial-state builders set up phase before its rollout begins. Dynamics collection. An agent session adds action perturbations to the solutions represented in the phase set and supplies physical-parameter ranges for the base scene. Before collection, the orchestrator checks the base solution using two 512-environment batches with the same seed and physical-parameter draws: one without action perturbations and one with them. Acceptance requires declared physical-parameter ranges, use of the noise argument, at least one success in the clean batch, positive fraction of perturbed steps, and at least one perturbed trajectory that succeeds and passes replay. The result is cached for that code fingerprint. After this check, scripted batches generate additional trajectories from the cells represented in the phase set, with physical and solution-parameter sampling and action perturbations enabled. Collection prioritizes cells with fewer accepted dynamics trajectories. Successful recordings are replaychecked after each batch. cell that produces no replay-verified success and has contributed no earlier dynamics success is removed from further collection. The final dynamics set retains the phase-set trajectories and adds further trajectories selected in turn across the contributing cells. Visual rendering. Every scene represented in the dynamics set must declare its cameras and visual-parameter ranges. An agent session supplies missing declarations or repairs declarations that fail short rendering check. The rendering queue contains trajectory-appearance pairs: the accepted trajectories at nominal appearance and the same trajectories under sampled appearance settings. The sampled passes also vary external camera poses. Each pass renders the declared camera views, and the nominal-appearance pass is processed before the additional appearance passes. Frames are generated by restoring recorded simulator states; physics is not re-simulated. Agent sessions and time limits. Each diversification stage has separate 12-hour time budget, covering agent work, simulation, replay checks, and rendering. session runs one coding-agent process with stage-specific brief, the runs working directory, and access to the simulator. Scene, strategy, and phase authoring sessions may use the remaining stage budget; individual repair, parallelization, perturbation, and visual-setup sessions are capped at 120 minutes. Trajectories generated during agent testing are eligible for selection under the same acceptance rules. During session, the orchestrator checks the recorded metadata every five minutes. When the metadata indicates that the stage requirements are met, it ends the session and performs the full acceptance check. If further work is needed, the next session continues from the existing files and notes. run stops if stage cannot finish within its time budget, and reports the failed stage. Execution and recovery. In our experiments, each run uses node with one RTX 4090 for the simulator, agent process, and orchestrator. The run periodically saves its code, records, and required trajectory files to durable storage. Restarting run resumes from this saved state without resetting its time budgets. Replay checks interrupted by time limit leave their pending trajectories ineligible for selection. If the language-model endpoint remains unavailable for ten minutes, the run pauses; paused time does not count toward the stage budget. D.3 DELIVERED DATASET Each generation run delivers collection of accepted trajectories and their rendered observations. Dataset construction follows the five diversification levels described above, while the number of trajectories contributed by each level and their relative proportions vary across tasks. The hierarchy provides an organizing framework for generation, without prescribing uniform allocation of demonstrations to each level. The policy-learning experiments in Section 4.2 evaluate increasing dataset sizes assembled through this framework; they do not isolate the contribution of individual diversification levels. For policy training, trajectories are converted to the LeRobot format at the recorded control rate. Visual observations come from the rendered camera views. Proprioceptive observations contain arm joint positions and gripper closedness. Training actions are commanded joint targets for positionmode controllers and achieved next-step joint positions for torque-mode controllers; the raw controller command is retained separately. The latter targets describe the motion actually achieved, in37 Preprint. cluding the effects of any perturbation. Each trajectoryappearance pair forms one dataset episode. Different appearance versions of the same physical trajectory share its state and action sequences. 38 Preprint.

sections.title: E VLA TRAINING AND EVALUATION DETAILS
sections.content: This section describes the datasets, model, finetuning recipe, and evaluation protocol behind the policy-learning results in Section 4.2. Dataset construction. For each task, we start from one verified coding-agent solution and generate demonstrations using EMBODIEDSWE-GEN. Every accepted trajectory passes the task grader and the open-loop replay check. The datasets combine task-dependent contributions from the five diversification levels, and we evaluate training sets containing 10, 50, 100, 200, and 400 episodes per task. For the generalization experiments, we construct training sets of 1,000 trajectories for each diversification setting. The agent-aided setting uses EMBODIEDSWE-GEN to vary scenes, solution strategies, and initial configurations, while the script-only baseline uses standard domain randomization, noise, and small initial-state perturbations. The control rate follows the registered task configuration and ranges from 15 to 60 Hz across tasks. Trajectories are converted to the LeRobot format. For the data-scaling experiments, we downsample each dataset into nested random subsets of episodes. We shuffle the episode indices once with fixed seed and take the first episodes for each subset size, so every subset contains all smaller ones. Normalization statistics are computed once on the full dataset and shared by all subsets, so that subsets differ only in the episodes seen during training. Observations and actions. The policy observes the RGB cameras declared by each scene at 480 640 resolution. Every scene provides wrist camera and one or two fixed cameras, such as front view together with side or overhead view. The proprioceptive state is 8-dimensional, consisting of the seven arm joint positions and gripper closedness. The language instruction is the scenes goal sentence. Actions are 8-dimensional joint targets at the scenes control rate, following the label convention in Appendix D.3. Following SmolVLAs input format, images are letterboxed to 512 512, state and action vectors are zero-padded to 32 dimensions, and the scenes cameras are mapped onto the pretrained models three camera slots, with any unused slot masked as missing. Model and finetuning. We finetune SmolVLA (Shukor et al., 2025) from the public smolvla base checkpoint, 450M-parameter model that pairs the first 16 layers of SmolVLM2-500M vision-language backbone with flow-matching action expert. The model predicts chunks of 50 actions, which spans 3.3 at 15 Hz and 0.8 at 60 Hz. We keep the vision encoder frozen and train the language-model layers together with the action expert. All runs use the same recipe. We train for 100k steps with batch size 64 using AdamW with learning rate 104, betas (0.9, 0.95), weight decay 1010, and gradient clipping at norm 10. The learning rate warms up over 1k steps and then follows cosine decay to 2.5 106 at step 100k. We save checkpoints every 20k steps and evaluate the final checkpoint. Intermediate checkpoints with partially decayed learning rate performed substantially worse in preliminary runs, so we do not report them. Each setting is trained with three random seeds. Evaluation protocol. Policies are evaluated closed-loop in the same simulator used for data generation. At each replanning step, the policy predicts 50-step action chunk, of which the first 10 actions are executed before the policy is queried again. For the data-scaling experiments, scene and physics settings are pinned from the training dataset, physical parameters take their nominal values, and each policy is evaluated on 32 episodes sampled from the scenes reset distribution (Appendix B). For the generalization experiments, policies are evaluated on 256 held-out configurations, covering semantically novel task instances and geometric configurations unseen in either training dataset. Evaluation seeds are disjoint from those used for data generation and paired across policies within each experiment. Episodes in which the simulator enters degenerate contact regime, such as bulb wedged in the socket rim that stalls the physics solver, are terminated and counted as failures rather than re-sampled. sections.title: TRAINING
sections.content: G.1 SYNTHETIC TASK CONSTRUCTION Robotics simulation tasks provide natural training environment for coding agents: outcomes are verifiable in the simulator, and multi-stage tasks come with well-defined partial credit. However, no existing resource provides such tasks at training scale. The closest, CaP-Gym (Fu et al., 2026), offers an evaluation harness rather than training corpus. We therefore design pipeline that scalably constructs new simulation environments from seed tasks, following the seed-and-mutate recipe of automated problem synthesis for coding agents (Zhou et al., 2025; He et al., 2026). Seed task selection. An agent asked to propose task with no anchor gravitates toward similar patterns (Zhou et al., 2025), so we start every construction by sampling seed task from RoboVerse (Geng et al., 2025), which aggregates tasks from many existing benchmarks. We sample at the task-file level and exclude locomotion and whole-body families. This leaves deduplicated pool of 194 distinct manipulation tasks spanning RLBench (James et al., 2019), LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023), ManiSkill (Mu et al., 2021), CALVIN (Mees et al., 2022), robosuite (Zhu et al., 2025), and others. The seed is handed to the agent as reference only, and the new task is implemented from scratch in our own task format. Task construction. The agent freely chooses how to mutate the seed task, including its objective, objects, and constraints, while ensuring that the new task is strategically different from its seed. This means that the solution code requires different plan and code structure, not just different parameters or minor changes. After authoring the scene, the agent writes teleport solution to the task, i.e., solution written as if any object could be teleported to any place. This is significantly easier to write than real-robot solution, while still useful for ensuring the legitimacy of the constructed task: teleportation handles only transport, while load-bearing interactions still go through the simulators contact dynamics. For example, to thread nut onto bolt, the solution teleports the nut to just above the bolt, then presses and twists it down the thread with applied forces until the scene reports success. This certifies that the interactions the task requires are physically achievable in the scene. The agent must also account for the embodiment when designing the task. Our coding-agent training focuses on manipulation with Franka arm, so beyond obtaining working teleport solution, the task construction agent must ensure that Franka arm, and more generally the target embodiment, can actually manipulate the objects in the way the task requires. After the teleport solution works, the agent writes the rubric for the task based on that solution. To check the rubrics legitimacy, the agent writes suite of rejection tests. In each test, the agent specifies scene state to be rejected, teleports the scene into exactly that state, and asserts that the rubric rejects it. The agent also writes task description for each task. Validation and acceptance. We validate each task through six checks: (1) rerun the agentauthored rejection tests and verify that bad states are correctly rejected; (2) verify that the null policy, which takes no actions, scores 0 under the constructed rubric; (3) check that scene randomizations vary across seeds and that the scene settles without numerical blow-ups; (4) verify that the rubrics score is non-decreasing throughout the teleport solution; (5) continue simulation after success first triggers and require success to persist, rejecting fly-through successes; and (6) use an LLM judge to assess task novelty, solution legitimacy, and task-description clarity. The judge checks whether the constructed task is strategically different from its seed, whether the teleport solution genuinely solves the task rather than exploiting environmental loopholes, and whether the task description is sufficiently clear to support solving the task. The generated environments currently serve only coding-agent training, since they have not gone through rigorous visual and physical validation and may carry artifacts such as interpenetrating geometry. These are tolerable for coding-agent training, where rewards are computed from simulator states, but not for VLA training, which consumes rendered frames. 42 Preprint. G.2 TRAINING SETUP AND RESULTS Training results. We train Seed-2.1-Lite with turn-level PPO on 400 environments produced by the pipeline above. Figure 20 shows the training results. Mean task reward roughly doubles, from 0.09 to 0.18, and the success rate rises from 2.7% to 7.5%. The gains arrive in two phases. During the first 100 steps the task reward is nearly flat while the format penalty shrinks from 0.14 to 0.06: the agent learns to finish episodes cleanly and to reason more briefly. Task reward begins to rise only after step 120, once penalties are mostly gone; over the same period the average episode shortens from 61 to 39 turns. Comparing steps 160 with steps 121180, 31 environments improve by more than 10 points in success rate. The reward standard deviation across episodes grows from 0.20 to 0.29 over the run, so the learning signal is not saturating at the cutoff. These dynamics indicate that the generated environments provide learnable, verifiable training signal for coding agents. We compare trajectories before and after RL training in Appendix H.6, illustrating what the agent learned to better solve robotics simulation tasks. External restrictions interrupted the project before held-out evaluation could be conducted. We therefore leave generalization of the post-trained agent to unseen tasks for future work. Figure 20: RL training curves. Agent interface. The coding agent executes Python programs in persistent Isaac Lab session, with Python variables and simulator state preserved between calls. It can inspect the benchmark source and receives execution logs and task-success feedback. separate vision-language model describes the initial scene and subsequent changes from fixed-camera images; the coding agent receives these descriptions as text. The arm uses operational-space control. Episodes. The agent receives the task description, robot configuration, and interaction rules, then works without human intervention. It may reset the environment or re-home the arm, while direct object-state edits, external force injection, scene modification, and scorer tampering are prohibited. Each episode allows at most 120 agent turns and 8,192 generated tokens per turn. It ends when the agent submits its final response or reaches turn or token limit. Reward. The reward is the final task rubric score in [0, 1], deducted by penalties for formatting errors and hacks identified by an LLM judge, such as scorer tampering. The total deduction is capped, with higher cap when tampering is detected. Episodes that exhaust their budget are scored using the simulator state at termination. RL algorithm. We use PPO with learned critic and generalized advantage estimation (GAE). GAE uses γ = 1, with λ = 0.95 for actor advantages and λ = 1 for critic targets. The lower and upper PPO clipping parameters are 0.3 and 0.35, respectively, with dual-clip parameter of 2. We use no KL penalty or entropy bonus. Rollouts are collected asynchronously. We apply importance-sampling corrections truncated at 2 to tokens generated by earlier policy versions, and exclude episodes whose policy weights are more than 16 training steps old. Optimization. Each training step uses batch of 128 episodes and performs one gradient update over the full batch, with the loss averaged over tokens. Both actor and critic use Muon, with learning 43 Preprint. rates of 2.7 106 and 3.5 106, respectively, five linear warmup steps, and weight decay 0.1. The critic is trained alone for five steps before actor updates begin. 44 Preprint.

sections.title: H QUALITATIVE ANALYSIS OF AGENT TRAJECTORIES
sections.content: In this section, we provide some qualitative analysis of agent trajectories, including an example of successful trajectory, and one representative example for each of the three failure modes discussed in Section 3.1. Excerpts in this section are quoted verbatim from the agents messages, its executed commands, the environments printouts, and its submission notes. H.1 SUCCESSFUL TRAJECTORY EXAMPLE We analyze the trajectory of Opus 5 on the coffee task. The agent reaches full solve (success=True, score=100) at minute 79 and spends the rest of its time hardening it. In this trajectory, the agent correctly makes the plan, fixes the failures it encountered, and delivered the verified solution. Stage 1. sections.title: I LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS
sections.content: In this section, we discuss the limitations and potential future directions of our work. Coding agents on dexterous hand tasks. EMBODIEDSWE-BENCH covers wide range of embodiments, but many others remain, such as dexterous hands with more fingers and joints. Whether and to what extent coding agents can control such embodiments, and how to guide and train them to do so, remains an open research problem. Boundary of coding-agent-to-robot distillation. Our synthetic task construction, solution generation, trajectory diversification, and VLA training components could together form pipeline for distilling coding-agent capabilities into robot policies. However, we have not yet run this pipeline end to end to study how much of the coding agents capability it can transfer to robot policies. Moreover, our environment generation pipeline does not optimize the visual quality of the generated scenes. This matters less for coding-agent training, where rewards are computed from oracle states and the rendered scenes need only roughly convey what is happening. For robot training, however, the divergence between generated and real scenes, and the need to guarantee that generated scenes are physically sound, become much more important. Another interesting question is the best use of the generated data for extremely complex tasks, e.g., for pre-training, for mid-training, or for RL / behavior cloning. We leave these as directions for future work. Training coding agents to better ground in visual observations. In Appendix G, we trained text-only model due to limited resources and because videos, even when subsampled into few frames, consume significant context length. How to train coding agents to better ground their code and actions in visual observations understanding the scene, tracking progress, and planning accordingly is left as future direction. Held-out evaluation of the trained agent. Appendix reports the training dynamics of RL post-training on the synthetic tasks. Due to computational resource constraints, we were unable to evaluate the trained checkpoint on held-out tasks before submission. The training curves and the qualitative analysis in Appendix suggest genuine behavioral improvement rather than degenerate reward exploitation, but quantifying these gains on held-out generated environments, and ultimately on EMBODIEDSWE-BENCH itself, is the most direct next step for this part of the work. **: Preprint.
